nameStory: This rose carries the name of William Sherard, an 18th-century English botanist who was passionate about cataloging European plants. The "downy" part of its name comes from the soft, fuzzy texture you'll feel when you gently run your fingers along the undersides of its leaves - they're covered in tiny hairs that give them a velvety feel.
description: Sherard's downy-rose is a medium-sized wild rose shrub that can grow up to 7 feet tall, though it's typically more compact than that. This European native has made its way to parts of New England, particularly Vermont, where it grows as a thorny shrub with distinctive grayish-green leaves. Like other wild roses, it produces lovely pink flowers in early summer followed by small red rose hips, but what sets it apart is those soft, downy leaves that feel almost fuzzy to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves have a distinctive grayish-green color and feel soft and downy on the undersides due to tiny hairs - run your finger underneath and you'll notice the velvety texture immediately

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pink five-petaled flowers appear in early summer, typically 1-2 inches across with the classic simple rose shape and yellow centers with many stamens

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a compact, thorny shrub up to 7 feet tall with arching branches armed with curved prickles that can snag clothing

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red to orange rose hips develop in late summer, oval-shaped and about the size of a small grape, persisting into winter

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Young stems are often reddish-brown with scattered curved thorns that hook backward, making them excellent at grabbing onto things

habitat: In New England, Sherard's downy-rose is found primarily in Vermont, where it grows in sheltered locations with full sun exposure. It prefers well-drained soils that stay somewhat moist, often appearing along woodland edges, old fields, or disturbed areas where it can get plenty of light but some protection from harsh winds.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their characteristic grayish-green color and downy texture, making identification possible even before flowers appear.
seasonality.summer: Pink flowers bloom in early summer, typically June, followed by the development of green rose hips that gradually ripen.
seasonality.fall: Rose hips turn bright red or orange and the leaves may take on yellowish tones before dropping, with the soft leaf texture remaining a key identifying feature.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny stems with persistent red rose hips make it identifiable, along with the distinctive reddish-brown bark on younger branches.

funFact: This rose is considered a botanical refugee - it's so rare in cultivation that even rose enthusiasts have probably never seen one in a garden, despite being described as an underappreciated gem that deserves more attention for its unique silvery foliage.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other downy-leaved roses, but Sherard's downy-rose is more compact and has grayer leaves than the similar Rosa tomentosa. The key memory trick: "Sherard's is shorter" - it stays more compact while other downy roses tend to get larger and rangier.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Sherard's downy-rose," this plant is sometimes listed scientifically as Rosa omissa in older field guides, which can cause confusion when trying to look it up. The name Rosa sherardii is now the accepted scientific name.
compareHints: Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage. While rugosa rose also has somewhat textured leaves, they're wrinkled rather than downy, and rugosa roses are much more robust plants overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
